label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
# Glenmore

I want to tell you all properly about the house in Glenmore, rather than have the news going around in bits on the phone.

I’ve agreed to sell it. The sale was agreed on 3 November and it closes on **15 January 2027**. I’m putting the date here plainly so that nobody has to hear it from someone else again.

I know some of you already heard, and not from me. Declan heard from his cousin Gráinne on WhatsApp. I’m sorry for that, and I’m sorry to the rest of you who found out second-hand too. I should have spoken to you myself. I especially regret not consulting Declan before I agreed the sale. He had every right to hear what I was thinking and to tell me what he thought.

Declan, I know you read these posts. I’m not angry with you. You rang me at two in the morning your time and said I was “selling Dad”. I know how much the house means to you and why the news hurt. I said things back that I shouldn’t have, and I’m sorry for those too. The door is open whenever you want to talk. I love you.

I want to explain why I’ve made the decision, what is happening to the house, and what we’re keeping. And I want to ask anyone who can make it to come out for a family day there on **Sunday 13 December**, before the house is cleared. I’ll come back to that below.

The house was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. It has been the old Mulkerrin place near Oughterard for as long as any of us can remember. Tom grew up there, and so much of his life is tied up with it that I understand why selling it feels like losing another part of him.

I feel that too. It would be easier to write this if I didn’t.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, of course, and the cattle were watching us. I can still see him standing there. I won’t try to improve the story by giving him a grand speech; the rain and the cattle are what I remember best.

Our own children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan would refuse to come out until his lips were blue, no matter how often he was called. Plenty of you will have your own memories of the place, some of them older than mine. The cousins who grew up away from Galway will have memories of visits and summers too. I know it has been part of more lives than just mine and Tom’s.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I’ve been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It’s forty minutes each way. At first I just kept doing it. There were things to look after and I wasn’t ready to think much beyond that.

But I need to tell you something I haven’t told anyone until now. Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door. There was frost on it. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up.

I didn’t tell you at the time. I don’t have a good reason, except that I didn’t want anyone worrying over me, and perhaps I didn’t want to admit to myself how frightened I’d been. Since then, I’ve been afraid of being alone at the house. I still went out, because the place needed checking, but I dreaded the possibility of falling again with nobody there.

There is also the work the house needs. Ó Flaithearta’s did a roof survey in September. The slates and the back chimney need attention, and the quote came to €38,000. There’s damp in the back bedroom as well. The septic tank needs replacing to sell the house to anyone anyway.

I’ve spent a lot of time going over those things, and over whether I could keep the house going somehow. The truth is that I cannot go on maintaining it. The journeys, the worry and the work have become more than I can manage.

None of that makes it an easy decision. Over the best part of two years, though, I’ve come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. I know that may not feel true to everyone just now. I’ve had time to get used to the thought, while some of you were handed the news without any warning. I should have given you that time too.

The couple buying the house are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in Glenmore; they’re not buying it as a holiday let.

The price was fair. It was less than the Dublin crowd offered in the summer, and I took the lower offer on purpose. It mattered to me that the house would be a home again. Tom always said it should have children in it, not be a museum. I’ve thought about him saying that a great deal.

The Joyces have also said that the family can come out and walk the land any time. I’m grateful to them for that. It won’t be the same as having the house in the family, and I’m not pretending it will, but I’m glad the children and the rest of us will still be able to go back there.

Some things are staying with us. The dresser is going to Úna’s. I’m keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. Those won’t be left behind when the house is cleared.

I know there may be other things you remember and want to see. That’s one reason I’d love you to come on **Sunday 13 December**, before we start clearing the house. We’ll have soup and sandwiches. Come if you can, and bring wellies.

There’s no need to make a ceremony of it. We can sit around, walk down towards the lake, look through things and tell the stories we remember. If you haven’t been out in years, you’ll be just as welcome as anyone. I know Boston and Perth are a long way away, and Leeds isn’t exactly around the corner either, so please don’t feel bad if you can’t get there.

Declan, I know you had been thinking of your summer visit. I’m sorry I didn’t talk to you before agreeing the sale. I should have. But I’m not willing to wait until the summer to sell, and I want to be honest about that as well.

I’m sure there are things some of you will want to ask, or say to me. You can ring me. I can’t promise we’ll all feel the same about this, but I should have let you into the conversation sooner, and I’ll listen now.

The house has held a great deal of our family’s life. It held Tom’s childhood, and a good part of ours together. I’ll miss knowing it’s there in the way it always has been. I’ll miss opening the door and seeing the familiar rooms, even on the days when I went out only to check that everything was all right.

But the sale is agreed and it closes on 15 January 2027. I hope, in time, you’ll understand why I’ve done it, even if you would have chosen differently. I hope too that some of you can come on the 13th of December, while the dresser is still in its place and we can all be together in the house once more.

Love to you all.
